items.item: A real Iceberg table under merge-on-read can use either position delete files (listing specific row positions to hide) or equality delete files (listing a value to hide wherever it appears), and Delta's deletion vectors are a third, file-local variant of the same idea -- all three share the property this topic measures (the data file itself is untouched until compaction), but differ in exactly how the hidden rows are identified.

at.out: the specific delete-file encodings (position vs equality vs deletion vector) named only; this topic's own toy model collapses all three into one delete-marker abstraction to isolate the shared mechanism

items.item: Orphan file removal (named in the syllabus clause alongside expire_snapshots) finds files that no snapshot references at all -- typically from a failed or aborted write -- and is a separate maintenance operation from expiring snapshots, which only removes metadata entries for snapshots that do still exist and are simply old.

at.out: orphan-file removal's own distinct purpose (cleaning up failed-write debris, not expiring old-but-valid snapshots) named only; this topic's own measurement models snapshot expiry and compaction, not an orphaned file from a failed write

items.item: Replicas (named in the syllabus clause alongside backups and Kafka topics) are a live, continuously-updated copy of a database, typically used for read scaling or failover, distinct from a point-in-time backup snapshot -- a DELETE that reaches the primary will eventually reach a replica through normal replication, but a replica paused or lagging behind the primary at the moment of deletion can hold the subject exactly as long as a stale backup would.

at.out: the replica case named only, as a variant of the same lagging-copy problem the backup and Kafka-consumer-lag measurements already demonstrate; this topic's own measurement covers a backup and a Kafka log, not a database replica specifically

items.item: The key-management cost side of per-subject crypto-shredding, named explicitly in the syllabus clause, is real at scale: a key per subject multiplies key-storage volume, requires a key lookup on every single read (not just at write time), and drives up the call rate against whatever key-management service holds the keys -- a cost this topic's own toy model, with two subjects, is far too small to demonstrate.

Crypto-shredding only erases what was actually encrypted under the deleted key; a plaintext copy made before encryption was ever applied -- an early extract, a log line, a debugging dump -- is completely untouched by deleting any key, which is why this topic's own CHAPTER.md explicitly leaves classification and discovery (an earlier topic) as the control that finds such copies in the first place.

at.out: the plaintext-copy limitation of crypto-shredding named only; this topic's own measurement encrypts all three copies from the start, so none of them is the untouched-plaintext case being warned about

items.item: Chapter 15's own 'GDPR erasure across lakehouse and backups' topic builds directly on this one, extending the single-table, single-topic, single-backup erasure this topic measures into a cross-system design problem requiring lineage lookup (finding every place a subject's data landed) and a unified proof across all of them.

at.out: Chapter 15's own cross-system extension named only as forward-pointing context; this topic's own scope is deliberately narrower, one table, one topic, one backup

items.item: Audit logging and tamper evidence, the skipped syllabus topic this topic's own CHAPTER.md names as what 'proving deletion from audit logs' would otherwise rely on, is replaced here by proving completion directly from the table's own metadata and the key store's deletion record -- a narrower but directly verifiable form of evidence that does not require a separate audit-logging system to exist.

at.out: audit logging's own would-be role in proving deletion named only; this topic's own evidence model uses the table and key store's own records instead, precisely because the audit-logging topic itself is not built

items.item: REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE), named in this topic's CHAPTER.md as one real compaction mechanism, and Delta's OPTIMIZE with a subsequent VACUUM are two vendor-specific commands that both perform the same underlying operation this topic's toy model calls 'compact': rewriting a data file to physically remove rows no longer referenced by any retained snapshot.

at.out: the specific vendor commands (REORG ... PURGE, OPTIMIZE plus VACUUM) named only; this topic's own `ToyTable.compact()` models the shared operation both commands perform, not either command's own syntax

items.item: GDPR Article 17's own exceptions (the right to erasure does not apply unconditionally -- for example, data needed for legal claims may be retained) mean that proving a system's technical capability to erase a subject is necessary but not sufficient; a real erasure request still requires a legal determination of which ground applies and whether an exception overrides it, a decision outside what any table-maintenance or key-deletion operation can make on its own.

at.out: GDPR Article 17's own stated exceptions named only; this topic's own measurement demonstrates the technical mechanism of erasure, not the legal decision of when erasure is actually required versus exempted

items.item: Retention policies written as versioned configuration -- a retention class per dataset, consumed by the same scheduled job that runs expire_snapshots/VACUUM/compaction -- turn a once-manual, easy-to-forget maintenance step into something a reviewer can read as code and a CI check can assert still matches what the table actually does, which is what separates 'we delete after some number of days' as a policy document from retention as an enforced, checkable property of the pipeline.

at.out: retention-as-code's own tie to the scheduled maintenance job named only; this topic's own measurement runs expire_snapshots and compact directly rather than through a scheduled retention-policy runner
